Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

This study has several strengths. It did a comprehensive, vigorous hypothesis test, by examining multiple experimental conditions under the same paradigm and with a large sample size. These results could help to reconcile the mixed findings in the literature. Their treatment of semantic relatedness is also thorough and appropriate. The conclusion is mostly accurate and justified. There are some methodological details that I think should be considered. Finally, the lack of neural evidence somewhat limits its conceptual advances.

My main suggestions are related to the methodological details, which I will detail below.

First, the current study used a retrieval-to-criterion learning paradigm, which is very efficient in achieving the desired learning outcome. Although I think this is appropriate for the initial learning of base pairs, it might introduce additional variances during the learning of second pairs that may complicate the explanations. As depicted in Figure S7, semantic relatedness facelifted new learning, resulting in fewer repetitions for strongly related pairs than weakly related pairs. Since this new learning also influences old memory, it is unclear whether the different repetitions also matter, in addition to semantic relatedness itself.

Second, the comparison between restudy and retrieval practice is very interesting and informative. The authors also made a good effort to match the exposure, by yoking each of 200 subjects to the exact learning order of subjects in the narrower stimulus set, 48-hr delay experiment. However, it is not clear how this was achieved, given the individual differences in the overall memory performance. This could be more complicated considering the memorability of a given pair also differs across subjects.

Third, the examination of memory dependence is also very interesting. I am curious how the dependence score is dissociated with the memory score? Still, one can imagine that this index might be less meaningful for subjects who performed very badly or very well in both tests, as their high dependence score might not reflect the true memory integration.

Fourth, the motivation of some experimental manipulations needs more justifications. For example, why did the author manipulate a narrower vs. a wider range of semantic relatedness? For the restudy vs. retrieval comparison, why the narrower stimulus set, 48-hr delay condition was selected?

My final comment is related to the theoretic account of the results. It seems that the interpretation of the results primarily relies on the recursive reminders account. Although I agree this is a reasonable choice, there are some issues that are worth mentioning. For example, this account might not explain the results under the ΔCue condition very well, and it is unclear whether these effects were mainly driven by the ΔTarget under the ΔBoth condition. It is also not readily transparent to me how it could account for the effect of study-test interval on the overall RI vs. RF patterns. Still, the authors did not discuss how it could account for the restudy vs. retrieval differences. Moreover, since there is no neural evidence to actually examine the reactivation during learning, it is my opinion that the current study did not provide direct evidence to support or refute this account, which somehow limits the conceptual advances of the current study. For the same reason, I am not sure if the neural model proposed in the discussion (Figure 7) is justified by the data.

Although this study used a large sample, some of the effects seem to be unreliable. For example, in figure S8, when both the narrow and wide conditions were merged, the effect of semantic relatedness show different trends, i.e., the regression line did not overlap. Did the authors also examine the strength of semantic association between the two words in each pair, and whether this could be a confounding factor that should be controlled in the analyses?

Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

Overall, this is a very solid and rigorous paper. The main contribution is to understanding the factors that determine behavioral measures of retroactive interference versus facilitation. In particular, when cue-target associations change (e.g., A-B to A-D), the question is how the degree of similarity between original and new cues and original and old targets will influence the relative interference vs. facilitation effects. This issue has a very long history in experimental psychology. The paper takes particular inspiration from a very influential idea from Osgood that interference/facilitation effects can be described along a continuous surface where cue similarity and target similarity are independent dimensions. The paper generally supports the ideas proposed by Osgood, but represents what is likely the most thorough empirical test of these ideas. Notably, whereas Osgood's original ideas were inspired by combining findings from many different experiments/papers/researchers, the current study packs all of the key experimental variables into a single, cohesive set of experiments.

Other strengths of the paper include relatively large sample sizes, consideration of the effects of delay (5 min vs. 48 hours) and consideration of the effects of retrieval practice vs. study. Additionally, although not a major point of emphasis in the paper, one of the interesting findings is that similarity between original and new items can protect older memories without increasing confusability (intrusions). This perhaps represents the most surprising result in the paper as the alternative prediction would be very reasonable (that semantic relatedness would increase intrusions). It seems difficult to pin down exactly why relatedness was protective against intrusions, but it is an intriguing result.

The biggest limitation in the paper is the amount of conceptual advance. As the authors note, Osgood's original ideas anticipated (most of) the key results in the current study-namely, the idea that facilitation and interference are a function of the similarity between original and new information. While the current paper provides a much more definitive investigation of this than is currently available in the literature, there have also been many papers since Osgood (nicely reviewed by the authors) that anticipate aspects of the current results. In particular, studies looking at integration or recursive reminders have clearly established that processes following initial encoding (of the base pairs) will impact the degree of interference and can even promote facilitation. In the current study, there is no direct evidence that integration or reminders occurred, but it is inferred that relatedness triggered reminders.

Taken together, the paper is likely to be of interest to those that study episodic memory in humans (and, in particular, those interested in memory interference). Given the influence of Osgood's original paper in the field of human learning and memory, this paper may also have substantial influence as a definitive test of Osgood's ideas. However, it is less clear whether the paper will have substantial influence outside this field.

The authors have addressed some of my comments, but not the others. In particular, they should have a more rigorous control of the effect of repetition time, and come up with a better theoretical framework.

Regarding comment #1, the authors did additional analyses to examine the effect of learning efficiency (as measured by the No. of repetitions) and memory. They found no significant linear correlations, and the relationship between semantic relatedness and RF/RI effect remained significant after controlling the learning efficiency.

According to the recursive reminder hypothesis the authors are trying to argue, each time new learning would reactivate the old association, which then affects the strength of old memory and its relationship with the new memory. The number of repetitions thus should have some effect, although it might not necessarily be in a linear fashion. We all know that repetitions do not linearly increase memory strength. Still, this effect should also be modulated by semantic relatedness, which determines the degree of reactivation of old memory. That said, I am not sure if there is a simple statistic method to control the effect of repetition time.

In addition, this confounding factor should also be considered when examining the effect of semantic relatedness on memory interdependency. It should also be considered when comparing the restudy and test conditions, which I will describe below.

Regarding comment #2, the authors acknowledged that the yoke between the repetition time between restudy and test was not perfect due to individual differences, but argued that this was sufficient to match the two conditions. To make this argument, I think the authors should show that the number of repetitions did not affect the overall results for both the test and restudy conditions. They have two choices to prove this. The first option is to randomly assign the number of repetitions to each pair and each subject, or use the group averaged repetitions for each pair (to account for the effect of semantic relatedness on subsequent learning) on every subject. The second option is to use a fixed number of repetitions for all subjects and pairs. I think the second option would be better, considering my comment #1.

Regarding my comment #3, the authors strongly argued that memorability and interdependence should theoretically be dissociated, with which I agree entirely. Nevertheless, with higher memorability, the chance of both items being remembered was also higher. I think a straightforward way to convince the readers is to calculate the correlation between memorability and interdependence and use memorability as a covariate while examining the result of interdependence.

For the Δboth condition, the authors found that Δcue and Δtarget relatedness have a different effect on interdependency and memorability. I agree with the authors that this result did complicate the result and the interpretation. Nevertheless, I think the result is interesting thus should be included and briefly discussed.

My last comment concerns the theoretical framework, which the first reviewer has also raised. In this revision, the authors briefly mentioned the recursive reminder hypothesis in the introduction but did not describe the hypothesis or the predictions. This introduces extra confusion about the relationship between the recursive reminder hypothesis and Osgood's predictions. What are the mechanisms underlying Osgood's predictions? Would the recursive reminder hypothesis support Osgood's predictions?

Moreover, both the recursive reminder hypothesis and Osgood's predictions deal with semantic relatedness. It is thus surprising that at the end of the Introduction, they were to examine several effects, such as the broad and narrow semantic association, the delay effect, the testing effect, and the effect of semantic relatedness on memory interdependency. Would the inclusion of these conditions help to falsify the hypothesis or predictions? The authors examined the semantic relatedness in different conditions separately but did not directly compare these conditions. They argued that this was because they were from different experiments. I am not sure if this argument is valid.

The authors introduce the testing effect to explain the delay effect and the difference between restudy and testing conditions. The testing effect, in my view, is mainly an observation, not an interpretation. Many possible mechanisms have been proposed and they are still under debate.

That said, I should note that this study examined a broad range of essential issues in RF and RI effects, and it is thus a challenge to come up with a simple theoretic framework to cover all of them. Meanwhile, I still think this study has provided critical empirical data for understanding the RF/RI effect. It is also laudable that they make the data open so that other researchers interested in this question could further examine it.

Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

The authors have thoughtfully responded to the comments I and other reviewers raised. I believe the revised manuscript is stronger and clearer. In particular, I think the theoretical framework is better established and the handling of the recursive reminders account is improved. This is a strong paper that has the potential to be of high impact.

results.result: The study employed a systematic experimental design across five experiments (N=1000 total) using paired-associate learning with counterbalanced conditions (No Δ, ΔTarget, ΔCue, ΔBoth, Control). Semantic relatedness was manipulated using two stimulus sets: a narrower set based on associative strength (AS, 0.03-0.96) and a wider set based on GloVe cosine similarity (-0.14 to 0.95), crossed with two test delays (5 min and 48 hr).
results.evaluation: The experimental design is thoroughly documented with appropriate counterbalancing, large sample sizes, and systematic manipulation of key variables. The within-subject design with counterbalancing across every five subjects controls for item-specific effects. The use of two different stimulus sets and delays allows for generalization of findings.

results.result: In the ΔTarget condition, semantic relatedness between targets produced retroactive facilitation that increased linearly with relatedness across most experiments. In the wider stimulus set with 5-min delay, retroactive interference occurred at very low relatedness but transitioned to facilitation with increasing relatedness. At 48-hr delay, low relatedness showed no effect while high relatedness produced significant facilitation.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C52 provide strong statistical evidence (all p<0.05 except ceiling effect) with regression analyses showing linear relationships. The interaction between relatedness level and delay is well-documented across experiments. The y-intercept analyses in C50-C51 appropriately distinguish between interference at low relatedness and facilitation at high relatedness.

results.result: Memory dependence between base and secondary pair targets increased with target relatedness (p<0.01) in all experiments except the narrower stimulus set 5-min experiment that showed ceiling performance. This indicates that semantic relatedness promotes interdependence where memories are remembered or forgotten together.
results.evaluation: The dependence measure (proportion of pairs both correct or both incorrect across subjects) is clearly defined and appropriately analyzed. Statistical significance is demonstrated in three of four experiments, with the exception explained by ceiling effects. The convergence of strengthening and interdependence effects supports the main theoretical claim.

results.result: Intrusions of secondary pair targets into base pair recall did not increase with target relatedness in any experiment (all p>0.08), and significantly decreased in the wider stimulus set 5-min experiment (p<0.001). This suggests that temporal order information was preserved rather than confused.
results.evaluation: The intrusion analysis directly tests an alternative hypothesis (source confusion) and finds evidence against it. The significant decrease in one experiment and null effects in others consistently argue against a confusion-based mechanism. This strengthens the interpretation that relatedness creates interdependence while preserving temporal context.

results.result: In the ΔCue condition, cue relatedness showed no significant relationship with base pair memorability in any experiment (all p>0.28), though marginally significant effects appeared in two experiments (p=0.085 and p=0.056). Memory dependence showed inconsistent relationships with cue relatedness across experiments.
results.evaluation: The null and weak effects are consistently reported across experiments with appropriate statistical tests. The inconsistency in dependence effects (significant in 2 of 4 experiments) is acknowledged. This pattern contrasts clearly with the robust ΔTarget effects, suggesting different mechanisms may operate for cue versus target relatedness.

results.result: In the ΔBoth condition, significant retroactive facilitation and memory dependence occurred only at high bivariate levels of both cue and target relatedness in the narrower stimulus set 48-hr delay experiment (p=0.001). Partial correlation analyses revealed dissociable effects: target relatedness predicted memorability (r=0.39, p=0.009) while cue relatedness predicted dependence (r=0.31, p=0.04).
results.evaluation: The cluster-based permutation testing approach is appropriate for the bivariate surface analysis. The specificity to one experiment (narrower set, 48-hr delay) is clearly documented. The partial correlation analyses in C62-C65 provide additional insight into dissociable mechanisms, though the sample size for these correlations (n=45 pairs) is modest.

results.result: In the study-only experiment (yoked exposure without retrieval practice), modest retroactive benefits emerged in the ΔTarget condition (target relatedness correlation p=0.02), but memory interdependencies did not increase with relatedness in any condition (all p>0.24). This contrasts with retrieval-to-criterion experiments where both benefits and interdependencies were observed.
results.evaluation: The yoking procedure appropriately controls for exposure duration. The dissociation between memorability effects (present) and dependence effects (absent) in study-only learning is clearly demonstrated. However, C175-C176 acknowledge limitations of the yoking procedure regarding individual differences, which could affect interpretation. The conclusion that retrieval promotes interdependence is reasonable but somewhat tentative.

results.result: In the wider stimulus set 5-min delay experiment, classical retroactive interference was replicated in the ΔTarget condition (No Δ>ΔCue=control=ΔBoth>ΔTarget), but this interference was specific to conditions of low average relatedness and short delay. The ΔBoth condition did not differ from control, suggesting these pairs were treated as novel.
results.evaluation: The replication of classical RI effects validates the experimental paradigm. The statistical pattern is clearly documented with appropriate post-hoc tests. The interpretation that ΔBoth pairs are treated as novel when relatedness is low is reasonable given the null effect, though alternative explanations (e.g., floor effects) are not fully ruled out.

results.result: Semantic relatedness accelerated secondary pair learning: higher cue relatedness produced faster learning in every experiment (all p<0.005), and higher target relatedness produced faster learning in all but one experiment. Additive cue+target relatedness effects were significant only in the narrower stimulus set experiments.
results.evaluation: The learning efficiency analyses (trials to criterion) provide converging evidence that relatedness scaffolds new learning. The consistency across experiments for cue effects and near-consistency for target effects is compelling. The specificity of additive effects to the narrower stimulus set aligns with the interpretation that low overall relatedness in the wider set leads to treating pairs as novel.

results.result: Partial correlations between relatedness and memorability controlling for secondary pair learning efficiency remained significant in all main analyses, indicating that retroactive facilitation effects did not depend on differential exposure during learning.
results.evaluation: This control analysis addresses an important alternative explanation. The persistence of effects after controlling for learning efficiency strengthens the interpretation that relatedness effects operate through memory mechanisms rather than simply through differential exposure. The statistical approach is appropriate.

results.result: The authors propose that semantic relatedness retroactively strengthens old associations while scaffolding new ones into well-fortified memory traces through a recursive reminders mechanism. According to this account, strong pre-existing associations increase the likelihood of spontaneously recollecting base pairs during secondary pair learning, creating interdependent memory traces while preserving temporal order information.
results.evaluation: This is the central theoretical interpretation, but it relies heavily on inference rather than direct measurement. The pattern of results (strengthening + interdependence + preserved temporal order) is consistent with recursive reminders, but the mechanism is not directly observed. Claims C135 acknowledges this limitation: the study did not manipulate instructions or collect in-the-moment reports of reminding. Alternative mechanisms cannot be fully ruled out.

results.result: Prior research on recursive reminders theory establishes that: (1) explicit or spontaneous reminders of past events during new learning can reduce interference or produce facilitation, (2) subjects must notice changes and recollect changed material for benefits to arise, and (3) reminders create interdependence between memories while preserving temporal context information.
results.evaluation: These claims accurately summarize prior literature with appropriate citations. The characterization of recursive reminders theory provides necessary context for interpreting the current results. However, this is a literature review rather than a novel finding from the current study.

results.result: The authors speculate on mechanisms underlying different conditions: weaker associations may lead to noticing but not recollecting changes; recursive reminders may slow forgetting rates; the ΔCue condition mechanism is unclear and may involve increased target availability rather than reminding; and changing both cues and targets may prevent recollection of pre-existing links.
results.evaluation: These are explicitly speculative interpretations (C96 uses 'speculate', C101 states 'less clear', C102 'could suggest'). While plausible, these mechanisms are not directly tested. The acknowledgment of uncertainty about ΔCue mechanisms (C101, C105) is appropriate given the weak and inconsistent effects.

results.result: The authors propose a neurobiological framework wherein pre-existing semantic relationships exist in neocortex while novel episodic associations are bound by hippocampus. High relatedness facilitates hippocampal reactivation of base pairs during secondary learning via cortical links, creating inter-hippocampal associations. This framework is supported by prior neuroimaging and animal studies showing reactivation during new learning predicts memory integration.
results.evaluation: This neurobiological framework is speculative (C121 is explicitly labeled as speculation in evidence_type). While it draws on legitimate prior neuroscience research (C114-C120), the current study includes no neural measurements. The framework is plausible and consistent with prior work, but represents a theoretical proposal rather than an empirically supported result from this study.

results.result: The results partially support Osgood's 1949 proposal: retroactive benefits increasing along the target identity line support the predicted RI-to-RF transition, and high bivariate relatedness in ΔBoth produces facilitation as visually suggested by Osgood's surface. However, the weak cue relatedness effects do not support predictions, the full RI-to-RF crossover was only found across experiments rather than within experiments, and multiple surfaces exist depending on overall relatedness and delay.
results.evaluation: This evaluation of Osgood's proposal is appropriately nuanced, acknowledging both support and discrepancies. The claim that there is 'no one surface' (C130) is well-supported by the different patterns across experiments. The assessment fairly represents both confirmatory and disconfirmatory evidence.

results.result: The authors acknowledge two key limitations: (1) the study did not dissociate semantic representations (distributional models) from associative relations (association strength), and (2) the study did not directly manipulate instructions or collect in-the-moment responses about recursive reminding.
results.evaluation: These are legitimate limitations appropriately acknowledged by the authors. The first limitation is important because semantic and associative relations can have different cognitive effects (C134 cites Thompson-Schill et al., 1998). The second limitation is critical for the recursive reminders interpretation, as the mechanism is inferred rather than directly measured.

results.result: Osgood's theoretical framework proposed three continuous dimensions along which relatedness influences memory: (1) along the ΔTarget line, RI should shift to RF as target relatedness increases from unrelated to identical; (2) along a line from identical to unrelated cues with unrelated targets, RI should disappear; (3) along the ΔCue line with identical targets, memory should improve from no change to maximum RF. These predictions form a three-dimensional surface.
results.evaluation: This accurately describes Osgood's historical theoretical proposal with appropriate citation. This provides essential context for the study's motivation and interpretation. However, this is background information rather than a novel result.

results.result: Prior research established that: ΔTarget learning typically causes RI due to response competition, but RI decreases when targets are semantically related; ΔCue learning produces little RI and can produce RF when cues are related; ΔBoth learning typically produces neither RI nor RF; and RI has been observed with modest relatedness at short delays, but longer-term memory with high bivariate relatedness has not been investigated.
results.evaluation: This accurately summarizes prior literature with appropriate citations and identifies the gap (C26) that motivates the current study. The characterization of prior work appears accurate based on the citations provided.

results.result: The high relatedness ΔTarget and ΔBoth conditions resemble 'closed-loop' learning configurations (A-B, B-C, A-C) from prior research, except that pre-existing semantic relationships close the loop rather than requiring de novo learning. This demonstrates interplay between semantic and episodic memory systems.
results.evaluation: This is a reasonable conceptual analogy to prior closed-loop research. The key insight is that pre-existing semantic relationships can serve a similar function to learned associations in creating interdependence. The interpretation about semantic-episodic interplay is well-supported by the pattern of results.
